He lives with his parents who are willing to support a medication change, and he is currently in regular outpatient contact with his case manager He is willing to commit to weekly FBC monitoring and to admission for induction if needed.

He has no history of cardiomyopathy and an echocardiogram shows preserved ejection fraction He understands clozapine monitoring and is willing to commence today Augmentation strategies were considered and not chosen His parents support the change.

data_table.Examination: BMI 28 kg/m2, no neurological signs, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal (WCC 6.4, neutrophils 3.8 x10^9/L), UEC normal, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms, troponin not measured (asymptomatic)
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 30 mg daily (current, 7 weeks)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Switch to clozapine, initiated under registered protocol with weekly FBC monitoring
options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as failure of two adequate trials (>=6 weeks at therapeutic dose, adherence confirmed) of two different antipsychotics; clozapine is the only evidence-based pharmacotherapy and Australian use requires patient registration with a clozapine monitoring service (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016; AMH 2024).

options.text: Add a second oral antipsychotic, amisulpride 400 mg, to the current aripiprazole regimen
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is not first-line for TRS and increases adverse effects without consistent efficacy benefit. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Trial a third oral antipsychotic, risperidone 6 mg daily, for 8 weeks first
options.rationale: Deferring clozapine after two adequate trials prolongs symptom burden, functional impairment and suicide risk. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as primary management of the persistent psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: ECT is for catatonia, severe depression with psychosis, or augmentation in clozapine-resistant; not first-line for TRS. Would be correct after clozapine failure (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Switch to a long-acting injectable formulation of aripiprazole given monthly intramuscularly
options.rationale: LAIs address adherence not efficacy; adherence has been confirmed, so issue is treatment resistance. Would be correct only with non-adherence (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Two adequate trials at therapeutic dose with confirmed adherence define treatment-resistant schizophrenia, for which clozapine is the only superior agent. In Australia, clozapine is dispensed via registered programs (e.g. ClopineCentral, ClozaConnect) with mandatory haematological monitoring (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016).
key_points: TRS criteria: failure of 2+ different antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration with adherence.
Clozapine requires baseline FBC, ECG and registration on a monitoring service.
Polypharmacy and switching to another non-clozapine agent are not first-line.
Clozapine reduces all-cause mortality and suicide in schizophrenia.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman has been on clozapine for 16 days, currently titrated to 200 mg nocte. She presents to the early-psychosis clinic feeling unwell for 36 hours with chest tightness on exertion, palpitations, a temperature of 38.2 degrees and a non-productive cough. There is no rash, no pleuritic pain, and no recent viral contact at home. She has no history of cardiac disease, no chest pain at rest, and observations show tachycardia.

Examination reveals a faint S3 gallop, no murmurs, clear chest sounds, and no peripheral oedema. Bloods today show WCC 7.8, neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L (within normal), CRP 78, troponin I 380 ng/L (laboratory upper reference 26 ng/L), eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118, no ST elevation, no PR depression.

data_table.Examination: Faint S3 gallop, clear lung fields, no oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 7.8, neutrophils 4.6, eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L, CRP 78, troponin I 380 ng/L (URL 26), ECG sinus tachycardia 118, no ST changes
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 200 mg nocte (day 16 of titration)

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Continue clozapine, add aspirin and review in 48 hours with repeat troponin
options.rationale: Continuing clozapine in suspected myocarditis is contraindicated (progression to fulminant HF); aspirin alone is inadequate. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, admit for cardiology review, and arrange urgent echocardiogram
options.rationale: In the first 4 to 8 weeks of clozapine titration, fever with tachycardia and rising troponin and CRP suggests clozapine-induced myocarditis; immediate cessation, admission, troponin trend, ECG, and echocardiogram are mandated (Source: AMH 2024; eTG Psychotropic: Clozapine adverse effects; TGA Clozapine PI).

options.text: Stop clozapine because the neutrophil count of 4.6 x10^9/L indicates impending agranulocytosis
options.rationale: ANC 4.6 is normal; agranulocytosis is under 0.5; clozapine is interrupted (Amber) at 1.0-1.5 and ceased at under 1.0. Would never be correct (Source: ClopineCentral).

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 100 mg and add atenolol 25 mg daily
options.rationale: Dose reduction without cessation does not address myocarditis; beta blockade can mask haemodynamic deterioration. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Treat empirically for community-acquired pneumonia with oral amoxicillin and doxycycline
options.rationale: Gallop, raised troponin and normal lung exam point to myocarditis not pneumonia; treating CAP without addressing cardiac picture is wrong. Would be correct only with documented CAP (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clozapine carries a 0.7-1.2% risk of myocarditis, peaking between weeks 2 and 4 of titration, and a lower lifetime risk of cardiomyopathy. The Australian protocol mandates baseline ECG, troponin, CRP and echocardiogram before commencement, then weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks. Presentation is non-specific: chest pain, dyspnoea, fatigue, fever, tachycardia, often with rising troponin (more than 2x ULN), rising CRP and ECG changes (T-wave inversion, ST depression). Eosinophilia is supportive but not required. Any troponin rise above twice ULN with symptoms mandates immediate clozapine cessation, admission for cardiology review, urgent transthoracic echocardiogram, and notification of the clozapine registry (CPMS or ClopineCentral). Recovery is usual with cessation; rechallenge has been done but requires specialist input and tight monitoring. Mortality from missed myocarditis is significant. Hypersalivation, fever and chest pain in the first month are clozapine until proven otherwise.
key_points: Myocarditis window: weeks 2 to 4 (most), up to 8 weeks.
Red flags: fever, tachycardia, troponin rise, CRP >50, dyspnoea, eosinophilia.
Agranulocytosis cut-offs (general): Green N >=2.0, Amber 1.5 to 2.0, Red <1.5 (some programs use 1.0).
Other clozapine adverse effects: hypersalivation, constipation/ileus, seizures, weight gain, hyperglycaemia.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis peaks at weeks 2-4 of titration with chest pain, dyspnoea, fever, fatigue and ECG changes; weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks is the Australian protocol. Troponin rise plus symptoms = cease clozapine, urgent echo (TGA Clozapine PI; AMH).

stem:
A 38-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg nocte for 4 years. His mother brings him to ED because he has not opened his bowels for nine days and has progressive abdominal distension, two episodes of vomiting today, and reduced oral intake. He has been on regular docusate and senna at home but his case manager added loperamide 1 week ago after he reported watery stools (in retrospect, likely overflow).

On examination he is mildly tachycardic, afebrile, and abdomen is distended, tympanic, with sluggish bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness without peritonism. He has no haematochezia. There is no past history of inflammatory bowel disease or abdominal surgery. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily. His clozapine FBC was normal three days ago His abdominal x-ray shows grossly dilated loops of large bowel with faecal loading and no free gas. The surgical registrar is reviewing him in ED.

data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen, sluggish bowel sounds, diffuse tenderness, no peritonism, no scars
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.2, Hb 138, Na 138, K 3.6, creatinine 92, lactate 1.4 mmol/L; AXR: dilated colon with no rectal gas, no free gas
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 400 mg nocte, docusate 50 mg BD, senna 15 mg nocte, loperamide 4 mg/day (1 week)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease loperamide, admit for IV fluids, NG decompression, surgical review and escalated laxatives
options.rationale: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility can progress from chronic constipation to ileus, megacolon and bowel perforation; loperamide is contraindicated, and management requires admission, decompression, surgical review and stepwise laxative escalation (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Clozapine adverse effects; AMH 2024).

options.text: Add an oral fibre supplement and arrange general practitioner follow-up in one week
options.rationale: Outpatient management with bulk laxative in established ileus risks bowel perforation; bulking agents can worsen impaction. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP; AMH).

options.text: Cease clozapine permanently because of constipation risk and switch to another antipsychotic
options.rationale: Abrupt permanent cessation of clozapine in stable treatment-responsive patient risks severe relapse; standard is to manage GI complication. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Order an urgent colonoscopy as the primary diagnostic investigation today
options.rationale: Colonoscopy in suspected ileus or megacolon carries high perforation risk; AXR and CT abdomen preferred. Would never be correct as first investigation (Source: ANZ Gastro).

options.text: Prescribe oral metoclopramide as a single 10 mg dose and discharge home
options.rationale: Metoclopramide is D2 antagonist that can cause EPSE and unlikely to reverse established large-bowel hypomotility; discharge unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) is under-recognised, can cause ileus, bowel ischaemia, perforation and death, and accounts for more clozapine-related deaths than agranulocytosis. The mechanism is anticholinergic and serotonergic suppression of GI motility, compounded by sedentary behaviour, sedation and constipating coprescribed medications. Risk is dose-related and persists lifelong. Australian guidance is daily bowel chart, prophylactic osmotic laxative (macrogol or lactulose) from initiation, and avoidance of constipating agents (loperamide, opioids, anticholinergics, tricyclics, antimuscarinic antihistamines). Any clozapine patient presenting with absent bowel motions for 3 days, abdominal pain, distension, vomiting or absent bowel sounds needs immediate admission, IV fluids, NG decompression, abdominal X-ray and surgical review. Treatment is aggressive osmotic and stimulant laxatives, prokinetics, and emergent surgery for perforation. CIGH is not an indication for stopping clozapine - the priority is treating the obstruction.
key_points: All clozapine patients need a documented bowel-monitoring plan and prophylactic laxatives.
Avoid loperamide, anticholinergics with high antimuscarinic load, and opioids where possible.
Overflow diarrhoea can mask severe constipation.
Mortality from ileus/perforation in clozapine cohorts exceeds that from agranulocytosis.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) is fatal in around 1 in 1000 patients per year; constipation, abdominal pain or vomiting on clozapine = immediate admission for IV fluids, NG decompression, surgical review and aggressive osmotic laxatives. Avoid loperamide, opioids and anticholinergics (eTG; Cochrane).

stem:
A 56-year-old man is admitted to the medical ward after presenting with a fractured wrist sustained in a fall. He drinks approximately 25 standard drinks per day and his last drink was 36 hours ago. He has a history of two previous withdrawal seizures and one prior episode of delirium tremens. He is currently tremulous, diaphoretic and reports tactile hallucinations of insects on his skin.

He is oriented to person and place but disoriented to time. His CIWA-Ar score is 22. He has no head injury. He was given 100 mg IM thiamine in ED. He has no known liver decompensation; LFTs show AST 110, ALT 65, INR 1.2 and albumin 36. He has no respiratory disease.

data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoresis, tactile hallucinations, oriented to person/place not time, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.6 mmol/L, Na 138, K 3.2, Mg 0.62 mmol/L, AST 110, ALT 65, INR 1.2, alcohol level 0
data_table.Medications: Thiamine 100 mg IM in ED, no regular meds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing his withdrawal?

options.text: Continue daily thiamine 100 mg orally and observe with hourly CIWA-Ar reassessment overnight
options.rationale: CIWA-Ar 22 is severe withdrawal; observation alone risks progression to seizures or DTs; oral thiamine is insufficient prophylaxis. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Symptom-triggered diazepam 10-20 mg PO 1-2 hourly titrated to CIWA-Ar plus IV Pabrinex
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing is the standard of care for severe alcohol withdrawal in Australian guidance; parenteral high-dose B-complex (Pabrinex) is required for Wernicke's prophylaxis in any heavy drinker with malnutrition risk, and electrolyte correction reduces seizure risk (Source: NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines; eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Commence oral carbamazepine 200 mg three times daily as the sole withdrawal agent
options.rationale: Anticonvulsants other than benzodiazepines are second-line and inferior for severe withdrawal; benzodiazepines are first-line. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Use an intravenous propofol infusion in a ward-based setting with bedside monitoring
options.rationale: Propofol infusion is for refractory DT in ICU; not appropriate on ward and not first-line. Would be correct in refractory DT in ICU (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Restart small amounts of oral alcohol to taper consumption over 5 days at home
options.rationale: Alcohol tapering is not used in AU inpatient practice; pharmacokinetic variability, hepatotoxicity and impaired titration make benzodiazepine-based withdrawal safer. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal in heavy daily drinkers typically begins 6-12 hours after last drink, peaks at 48-72 hours, and resolves over 5-7 days. Severity is stratified with the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol revised), with score over 15 indicating severe withdrawal. Australian standard management is symptom-triggered diazepam dosing (rather than fixed-schedule) titrated to CIWA-Ar - typically 10-20 mg PO every 1-2 hours - which has the same efficacy with lower total dose and shorter inpatient stay. Concurrent parenteral B-complex (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS for 3-5 days) prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy, with magnesium replacement and aggressive electrolyte correction (potassium, phosphate). Prior seizures, prior delirium tremens, comorbid medical illness, or CIWA-Ar above 25 lower the threshold for ICU. Discharge planning includes naltrexone or acamprosate, counselling and ongoing engagement with addiction services.
key_points: Pabrinex (high-dose IV thiamine + B-complex) BD for 3 to 5 days for at-risk patients.
Oral thiamine alone is inadequate in alcoholic malnutrition.
Symptom-triggered diazepam outperforms fixed-dose regimens.
Correct hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia to reduce seizure risk.
explanation.pearls: Symptom-triggered diazepam (10-20 mg PO every 1-2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar) plus IV Pabrinex (2 pairs TDS for 3-5 days) is the Australian protocol for severe alcohol withdrawal; prior seizures or DTs lower the threshold for ICU admission (NSW Health; eTG Addiction).

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem:
A 62-year-old homeless man is brought to ED after being found drowsy in a park. He has a 30-year history of heavy daily alcohol use and weighs 54 kg with a BMI of 18. He is hypothermic at 35.4 degrees and capillary glucose is 2.8 mmol/L. The triage nurse hangs an IV bag of 5% dextrose. Forty minutes later the resident notes ataxia, horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, and ophthalmoparesis with bilateral abducens weakness.

He is intermittently confused but rousable. He has had no head trauma. CT brain shows no acute lesion. He has not received any thiamine yet. Sodium is 134, potassium 3.4, magnesium 0.58 mmol/L, INR 1.3, AST 95, ALT 50 The triage nurse asks whether the dextrose infusion should be paused before any thiamine is given, and whether IM 100 mg thiamine is sufficient He has no head trauma history.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.4, HR 98, BP 108/62, RR 16, SpO2 98%, BSL 2.8 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Ataxic, horizontal nystagmus, bilateral CN VI weakness, confused, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Na 134, K 3.4, Mg 0.58 mmol/L, INR 1.3, AST 95, ALT 50, CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV high-dose B-complex (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS), correct magnesium, then continue dextrose
options.rationale: Suspected Wernicke's requires immediate parenteral high-dose B-complex (Pabrinex) before or with any glucose; magnesium is a cofactor and must be corrected for thiamine to be effective. Australian dosing is 2 pairs IV TDS for 3 to 5 days (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Wernicke's encephalopathy; NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Continue dextrose, give a single 100 mg intramuscular dose of thiamine, then monitor
options.rationale: Standard 100 mg IM thiamine is inadequate for established Wernicke's; high-dose parenteral B-complex BD-TDS for several days required. Would be correct only for prophylaxis not established WE (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Hold any further IV glucose and commence intravenous magnesium sulfate as monotherapy
options.rationale: Correcting hypoglycaemia must continue with concurrent thiamine; magnesium without thiamine does not reverse Wernicke's. Would be correct as part of full regimen, not as monotherapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange an urgent MRI brain before commencing any pharmacological replacement therapy
options.rationale: Wernicke's is clinical diagnosis; delay for imaging risks permanent Korsakoff amnesia; treatment must be empirical. Would never be correct (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Commence oral thiamine 300 mg daily without any parenteral B-vitamin therapy
options.rationale: Oral absorption is unreliable in chronic alcohol use and inadequate for established encephalopathy; parenteral high-dose B-complex required. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Wernicke's encephalopathy is an acute, treatable, frequently missed thiamine-deficiency syndrome - autopsy series suggest it is recognised antemortem in under a third of cases. The full triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion is present in fewer than 20% of patients, so any malnourished, alcohol-dependent, hyperemetic or bariatric-surgery patient with unexplained neurological signs warrants empirical thiamine. Glucose without preceding or co-administered thiamine pushes pyruvate into glycolysis and precipitates or worsens encephalopathy. Australian practice is high-dose parenteral B-complex (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS for 3-5 days, then taper) plus magnesium replacement (cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes). Untreated, 80% develop Korsakoff's amnestic syndrome and 20% die. Continue oral thiamine 100 mg daily at discharge with alcohol-use disorder management.
key_points: Empirical high-dose parenteral B-complex (Pabrinex) for any at-risk patient before glucose.
Magnesium is a thiamine cofactor and must be replaced.
Untreated Wernicke's progresses to irreversible Korsakoff syndrome.
Caine criteria: 2 of 4 - dietary deficiency, oculomotor abnormalities, cerebellar dysfunction, altered mental state.
explanation.pearls: In suspected Wernicke's, give Pabrinex (IV thiamine 250 mg) BEFORE any glucose; glucose-first precipitates encephalopathy by accelerating thiamine consumption in glycolysis. Australian protocol is 2 pairs IV TDS for 3-5 days (eTG; NSW Health alcohol withdrawal).

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem:
A 49-year-old teacher with alcohol use disorder presents to her GP seeking pharmacological help to stay abstinent. She completed a community-supported withdrawal three weeks ago and has been alcohol-free since then. Her main concerns are recurrent strong cravings and a high-risk family wedding in two weeks. She has chronic back pain managed with paracetamol only and no current opioid prescription.

She has no significant liver impairment (LFTs and INR normal), no renal impairment, and a normal ECG. She does not have a history of severe liver disease or active hepatitis. She is highly motivated, lives with a supportive partner, and attends weekly counselling. She has tried mutual-support groups previously without sustained benefit. She is otherwise well and not pregnant; she uses an IUD for contraception She has read about acamprosate, naltrexone and disulfiram and asks the GP to recommend the option most likely to help her control cravings, particularly given the high-risk family wedding in two weeks where alcohol will be present She has no opioid prescription and no current opioid use, and she does not want disulfiram because of the wedding.

data_table.Examination: BMI 24, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, normal mental state, no other comorbidities
data_table.Investigations: AST 28, ALT 24, GGT 38, bilirubin 12, INR 1.0, eGFR >90 mL/min, FBC normal
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g QID PRN, no opioids

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate as first-line maintenance treatment to support abstinence?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg orally daily
options.rationale: Naltrexone is first-line for AUD maintenance in patients not on opioids, reduces cravings and heavy-drinking days, and is appropriate where craving is the dominant symptom; it is contraindicated in current opioid use (Source: RACP/RANZCP Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of AUD; eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).

options.text: Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily
options.rationale: Acamprosate is equally valid first-line (best for sustaining abstinence already achieved); naltrexone has stronger craving evidence. Would be correct when abstinence already achieved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Disulfiram 200 mg daily
options.rationale: Disulfiram requires high motivation, supervised dosing and acceptance of aversive reaction; second-line. Would be correct after first-line failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg three times daily for ongoing craving
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are for acute withdrawal only; ongoing use risks cross-dependence and is not maintenance therapy. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Topiramate 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Topiramate has some evidence but is off-label in AU and third-line; cognitive adverse effects notable in working woman. Would be correct only after first-line failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Naltrexone and acamprosate are the two first-line, PBS-listed pharmacotherapies for alcohol use disorder in Australian practice. Naltrexone (50 mg orally daily) is a mu-opioid antagonist that reduces the reinforcing effect of alcohol, decreasing cravings and heavy drinking - effective whether the goal is abstinence or reduction. Contraindications are current opioid use (including methadone or buprenorphine maintenance), opioid withdrawal (precipitates severe symptoms), acute hepatitis, and severe liver dysfunction (Child-Pugh C). Acamprosate (666 mg TDS) modulates NMDA and GABA-A receptors and supports continued abstinence after withdrawal; it requires the patient to be alcohol-free at initiation. The two can be combined for additive effect. Disulfiram (200-400 mg daily aversion therapy) is second-line and requires supervised dosing, cardiac and hepatic clearance, and committed motivation. Topiramate and gabapentin are off-label options. All pharmacotherapy is delivered alongside psychosocial intervention.
key_points: Confirm patient is opioid-free (urine drug screen) before naltrexone.
Acamprosate: maintain abstinence; dosed TDS by weight; renal excretion.
Disulfiram: requires supervised dosing and motivation; CVS/hepatic risks.
Pharmacotherapy is always combined with psychosocial support.
explanation.pearls: Naltrexone 50 mg daily is first-line PBS-listed AUD pharmacotherapy in Australia - reduces cravings and heavy drinking by acting at the mu-opioid receptor. Contraindicated in current opioid use, opioid withdrawal, severe liver dysfunction (RACGP/RANZCP AUD).

stem:
A 58-year-old man has chronic alcohol use disorder and has failed adequate trials of naltrexone (compliance confirmed by his partner) and acamprosate over the past 12 months, with ongoing harmful drinking. He has well-compensated alcohol-related liver disease (Child-Pugh A; AST 80, ALT 55, INR 1.2, albumin 35, no ascites or encephalopathy). He has stable ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI two years ago and a normal ECG today.

He is highly motivated, lives with a supportive partner who can supervise daily dosing, and attends a specialist alcohol service. Echocardiogram shows preserved ejection fraction 58%. He has no respiratory disease. He understands and accepts the disulfiram-ethanol reaction The specialist alcohol clinician is keen to start a relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy today; the patient has consented to the disulfiram-ethanol reaction warning leaflet. The cardiology team has flagged that hypotension and arrhythmia risk are the main concern with disulfiram.

data_table.Examination: Stable, no signs of decompensated liver disease, normal mental state
data_table.Investigations: AST 80, ALT 55, INR 1.2, albumin 35, no ascites; ECG normal; EF 58%
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, metoprolol 25 mg BD; naltrexone and acamprosate trialled previously

lead_in: Which factor most strongly contraindicates initiating disulfiram in this patient?

options.text: Pre-existing ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary intervention
options.rationale: Significant cardiovascular disease (including ischaemic heart disease, severe hypertension, recent MI or stroke) is a contraindication to disulfiram because the disulfiram-ethanol reaction can precipitate severe hypertension, arrhythmia and cardiovascular collapse (Source: eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).

options.text: Mild compensated liver disease with Child-Pugh A staging
options.rationale: Severe hepatic impairment is contraindication; compensated Child-Pugh A is caution requiring LFT monitoring, not absolute bar. Would be correct only with severe impairment (Source: AMH).

options.text: Concurrent metoprolol therapy used for rate control
options.rationale: Metoprolol has no specific contraindication with disulfiram. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

options.text: Patient age over 55 years at initiation of disulfiram
options.rationale: Age alone is not contraindication; risk-benefit individualised. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

options.text: Concurrent atorvastatin therapy used for secondary prevention
options.rationale: No clinically significant interaction precluding co-prescription of atorvastatin with disulfiram. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Disulfiram is a second- or third-line pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder used when first-line agents (naltrexone, acamprosate) have failed in motivated patients with committed abstinence goals. It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so any alcohol ingestion produces acetaldehyde accumulation with flushing, headache, palpitations, nausea, vomiting and hypotension - the disulfiram-ethanol reaction (DER). The DER can be fatal in patients with cardiovascular disease, severe hepatic failure or significant electrolyte derangement; these are absolute contraindications, alongside pregnancy, psychosis (can precipitate decompensation), and inability to consent to supervised aversion therapy. Even hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrup, vinegar, communion wine, fermented sauces) can trigger DER. Baseline ECG, LFTs, and informed consent documentation are mandatory. Standard dose 200-400 mg daily, ideally with supervised administration (partner or pharmacy daily pick-up). Hepatotoxicity in 1 in 30000 requires monthly LFTs initially.
key_points: Avoid in IHD, severe HTN, recent MI/stroke, severe liver failure, psychosis.
Counsel about all ethanol sources (cough mixtures, mouthwash, aftershave, sauces).
LFTs at baseline, 2 and 6 weeks, then 3 to 6 monthly.
Reaction onset is 10 to 30 minutes after ethanol, can last several hours.
explanation.pearls: Disulfiram contraindications: significant cardiovascular disease (the disulfiram-ethanol reaction can cause hypotension, MI, arrhythmia, death), severe hepatic failure, pregnancy, psychosis, and inability to consent to supervised aversion therapy (eTG Addiction; AMH).

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with a 6-year history of injecting heroin presents to a community OST clinic seeking opioid agonist treatment. She last used heroin 12 hours ago. She has tested positive for HCV antibody (RNA pending) and her LFTs show ALT 84, AST 60. She has no other psychiatric medications and no significant medical comorbidity. Her observations are normal. COWS score on assessment is 14 (moderate withdrawal) with pupil dilation, sweating, yawning, mild rhinorrhoea, anxiety and bone aches.

Urine drug screen is positive for opioids only. She is unable to attend a clinic for daily supervised dispensing because she works variable shifts but can attend twice weekly. She has no respiratory disease, no QT-prolonging medications, and an ECG today shows QTc 410 ms.

data_table.Examination: Mydriasis, diaphoresis, restless, no signs of overdose; venepuncture marks both antecubital fossae
data_table.Investigations: COWS 14, AST 60, ALT 84, ECG QTc 410 ms, urine drug screen positive opioids only, HCV antibody positive (RNA pending)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in induction?

options.text: Sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone 4 mg now, top-up 2 to 4 mg in 2 hours if withdrawal persists
options.rationale: Buprenorphine is preferred over methadone for community induction because of lower overdose risk, capacity for unsupervised takeaway doses earlier, and shorter induction; it must only be given once moderate withdrawal is established (COWS >=12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal (Source: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence; eTG Addiction).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Commence methadone 60 mg orally today as the safer first-day community induction dose
options.rationale: Methadone induction starts low (20-30 mg, no more than 40 mg day 1) due to long half-life and accumulation risk; 60 mg day 1 has caused fatal overdoses. Would never be correct (Source: NSW Health Methadone Guideline).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Wait until she has been opioid-free for 24 hours and then commence oral naltrexone
options.rationale: Oral naltrexone has very high relapse rates in opioid dependence and is not first-line maintenance; cannot start until 7-10 days opioid-free. Would be correct in highly motivated abstinence-focused patients (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Give intramuscular naloxone now to confirm opioid dependence before any induction begins
options.rationale: Naloxone reverses overdose, not for confirming dependence; deliberate precipitation of withdrawal is unethical. Would never be correct (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Commence sublingual buprenorphine 16 mg as a single first dose to suppress withdrawal rapidly
options.rationale: Day-1 buprenorphine should start at 2-8 mg with cautious top-up; 16 mg risks oversedation. Would be correct only at later titration (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine-naloxone induction in established moderate withdrawal (COWS >=12) is preferred for community OST, especially for patients with limited capacity for daily supervised dispensing. Methadone is started low and titrated slowly because of accumulation and overdose risk (Source: NGMA; eTG Addiction).
key_points: Methadone day 1: 20 to 30 mg, max 40 mg; steady state at 5 days.
Buprenorphine: lower overdose risk, ceiling on respiratory depression, faster stabilisation.
Precipitated withdrawal: occurs if buprenorphine given too early.
ECG before methadone if dose >100 mg or QT-prolonging meds; review at 1 month.

sources.label: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

stem:
A 45-year-old man on methadone 80 mg daily for 3 years presents to his GP with new-onset palpitations. He was admitted for community-acquired pneumonia 10 days ago and discharged on azithromycin 500 mg daily (now stopped) and oral fluconazole 200 mg daily (continuing) for oropharyngeal candidiasis. He has also been taking diphenhydramine for sleep. Resting ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 78 with QTc 510 ms (previously 430 ms before admission).

He has no chest pain, no syncope and no electrolyte derangement. Electrolytes are normal including potassium 4.1 and magnesium 0.85. He has not increased his methadone dose. He denies non-prescribed drug use and urine drug screen is positive only for methadone and benzodiazepines (he disclosed temazepam supplied by a friend)

data_table.Examination: No oedema, no murmurs, clear chest, no syncope
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 510 ms (was 430), K 4.1, Mg 0.85, eGFR >90, LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Methadone 80 mg daily, fluconazole 200 mg daily, diphenhydramine PRN, temazepam (illicitly sourced)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop fluconazole and diphenhydramine, counsel against benzodiazepines, consider methadone dose reduction or switch
options.rationale: Fluconazole inhibits methadone metabolism (CYP3A4/CYP2B6) and prolongs QT; diphenhydramine adds anticholinergic load and QT effect; the priority is removing the offending agents, addressing benzodiazepine use, and re-evaluating with repeat ECG, with a switch to buprenorphine if QT remains prolonged (Source: NGMA; eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Continue the current regimen unchanged and review the patient in 4 weeks with a repeat ECG
options.rationale: QTc 510 ms carries significant torsades risk and demands prompt action; passive review is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

options.text: Increase methadone to 100 mg daily to improve compliance and stabilise opioid receptors
options.rationale: Increasing methadone worsens QT prolongation and overdose risk, particularly with co-ingested benzodiazepines. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Cease methadone abruptly today and commence naltrexone after 24 hours of opioid abstinence
options.rationale: Abrupt methadone cessation precipitates withdrawal and relapse; naltrexone cannot start until 7-10 days opioid-free. Would never be correct (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.text: Add an oral beta-blocker (atenolol 25 mg daily) to reduce torsades de pointes risk acutely
options.rationale: Beta-blockers reduce risk in congenital LQTS but not standard response to drug-induced QT prolongation; correct approach is to identify and remove QT-prolonging drugs. Would be correct only in congenital LQTS (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Methadone prolongs QTc and accumulates when CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, HIV PIs) are introduced; combined with benzodiazepines, overdose risk rises. Australian OST guidance recommends ECG before methadone if dose >100 mg or QT-prolonging meds, repeat at 1 month and after dose or interacting-drug changes (Source: NGMA).
key_points: QT-prolonging interactions: azoles, macrolides, ondansetron, SSRIs, antipsychotics, HIV PIs.
QTc >500 ms is a strong indication to switch from methadone to buprenorphine.
Concurrent benzodiazepines markedly increase overdose mortality.
Naloxone supply and overdose education are part of routine OST care.

sources.label: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

stem:
A 26-year-old man is brought to ED by police after acting bizarrely in a shopping centre, smashing a window and shouting at unseen individuals. He has used crystal methamphetamine for 18 months and admits to using last night. On arrival he is pacing, sweating, threatening staff verbally, and intermittently striking the wall. He has dilated pupils, marked tachycardia, hypertension and a low-grade fever.

He has not had any seizures, no head injury, and there is no other identified medical contributor. He is on no regular medication. Initial verbal de-escalation has failed and he is now attempting to leave. Capillary glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. Bloods are pending. The patient weighs approximately 80 kg, has no airway concerns at present, and continuous cardiac monitoring can be commenced in the high-acuity area

data_table.Examination: Mydriasis, diaphoresis, agitated, hyper-vigilant, no focal neurology, no head injury, no obvious overdose features
data_table.Investigations: BSL 6.8 mmol/L, urine drug screen pending, ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 430 ms

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological management of his acute behavioural disturbance?

options.text: IM droperidol 10 mg with cautious midazolam 2.5 to 5 mg titrated, in a monitored area
options.rationale: Australian ED guidance for severe stimulant-related acute behavioural disturbance recommends parenteral droperidol with cautious adjunctive midazolam in a monitored setting, reflecting NSW Health protocols; this rapidly controls agitation while minimising oversedation (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance; eTG Toxicology).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.text: Oral diazepam 20 mg single dose, awaiting effect over the next 60 minutes
options.rationale: Oral medication is unsafe and impractical for severe ABD with imminent harm; parenteral in monitored area required. Would be correct only for mild agitation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.text: Intramuscular ketamine as first-line for acute behavioural sedation
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for refractory cases when droperidol and benzodiazepine have failed (laryngospasm, hypertension, airway risks). Would be correct only as refractory (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.text: Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg as a single dose without concurrent benzodiazepine
options.rationale: IV haloperidol carries higher QT/torsades risk than IM droperidol and is not preferred in AU ABD protocols. Would be correct only if droperidol unavailable (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.text: Physical restraint without any pharmacotherapy, awaiting natural resolution over hours
options.rationale: Prolonged physical restraint without sedation risks asphyxia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and sudden death in stimulant intoxication. Would never be correct (Source: ANZICS).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance (ABD) from methamphetamine or other stimulants presents with severe agitation, paranoid psychosis, hypertensive crisis, hyperthermia, and risk of self-harm or harm to others. The NSW Health ABD Guideline and eTG Toxicology recommend IM droperidol 10 mg as first-line in a monitored ED resuscitation bay - droperidol has rapid onset, sedates without dropping BP, and is well-tolerated. Cautious IM midazolam 2.5-5 mg can be added for ongoing agitation, titrated to effect to avoid respiratory depression. Restrain only if needed for safety, with continuous monitoring of vital signs, SpO2, ECG, and core temperature. Anticipate stimulant complications: hyperthermia above 39 requires active cooling, rhabdomyolysis warrants CK and fluid resuscitation, hypertensive emergency may need short-acting vasodilator, and acute coronary syndromes occur even in young patients. Avoid haloperidol IV (QT prolongation in cocaine and methamphetamine). Once stabilised, brief psychiatric assessment, social supports, and addiction medicine referral.
key_points: Treat the patient, monitor airway/breathing/circulation continuously after sedation.
Cool, hydrate, assess for rhabdomyolysis (CK), check ECG and electrolytes.
Avoid pure beta-blockade for stimulant hypertension (unopposed alpha effect); use benzodiazepines first.
Methamphetamine-induced psychosis typically resolves within 1 week with abstinence; persistent symptoms warrant psychiatric review.
explanation.pearls: Severe acute behavioural disturbance from methamphetamine: IM droperidol 10 mg in a monitored area, with cautious IM midazolam 2.5-5 mg titrated for agitation. Anticipate stimulant hyperthermia (above 39 = active cooling), rhabdomyolysis, dysrhythmia (NSW Health ABD).

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

stem:
A 33-year-old woman is brought to ED by her partner. She has bipolar disorder and stopped lithium 3 weeks ago. Over the past 5 days she has slept 2 to 3 hours per night, has been spending savings on unnecessary purchases, and is now describing herself as 'chosen to save the city'. She has not slept in 36 hours and is pacing the ED.

There is no current suicidal ideation or thoughts of harming others. She has no medical comorbidity, and a UDS and bloods are unremarkable. On MSE she is dressed flamboyantly, pressured in speech, with flight of ideas and grandiose delusions. She insists she is not unwell and refuses any treatment, including reinstating lithium. Her partner is present and supportive, and the community mental-health team has a current case manager

data_table.Examination: Elevated mood, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, no current SI/HI, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH normal, urine drug screen negative, beta-hCG negative, lithium level <0.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium ceased 3 weeks ago by patient; no current medications

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 (or equivalent state Act)?

options.text: Detain under the MHA assessment schedule and admit to a declared mental health facility for review
options.rationale: She meets criteria as a mentally ill person (presence of mental illness, behaviour requires treatment to protect her from serious harm including risk to her health/safety such as exhaustion, financial harm) and is refusing voluntary admission; the MHA assessment schedule and admission to a declared facility for AMO review is the appropriate pathway (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP).

options.text: Discharge home with her partner and arrange outpatient review with the case manager tomorrow
options.rationale: Severe sleep deprivation, escalating manic behaviour and refusal of treatment make outpatient unsafe in next 24 h. Would never be correct (Source: NSW MHA).

options.text: Apply common-law restraint and sedate her in the ED without using the Mental Health Act
options.rationale: Common-law restraint is for emergency intervention to prevent immediate harm, not primary framework for ongoing detention and treatment. Would be correct only briefly during emergency (Source: NSW MHA).

options.text: Make a community treatment order today without proceeding to any inpatient admission
options.rationale: CTOs are made by MHRT following inpatient assessment with specific procedural steps; cannot be made directly from ED. Would never be correct (Source: NSW MHA).

options.text: Document her refusal of care and allow discharge from ED against medical advice
options.rationale: She lacks capacity to refuse treatment due to grandiose delusions and lack of insight; MHA exists to address this. Would never be correct (Source: NSW MHA).

explanation.summary: Acute mania with refusal of treatment and risk to self meets criteria for involuntary admission under state MHAs. The least-restrictive principle still applies, but inpatient assessment is required before any community treatment order can be considered (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).
key_points: Schedules/forms vary by state but principles are similar: presence of mental illness, risk of serious harm, no less restrictive option.
Common-law restraint is for immediate, brief safety - not ongoing treatment.
Community treatment orders follow tribunal processes after inpatient assessment.
Capacity is decision-specific and is impaired by acute mania with grandiose delusions.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been treated with first-generation antipsychotics for 25 years (most recently haloperidol 10 mg daily) and is being reviewed in the outpatient clinic. She has new-onset chewing movements, lip-smacking and occasional protrusion of the tongue for the past 4 months, occurring while not consciously moving and persisting during conversation. She has no oculogyric movements, no postural instability.

AIMS examination scores her in the moderate severity range with involuntary orofacial movements. She is currently otherwise stable in her mental state. There is no history of cognitive impairment, and she has no recent change in medication. She has tried benztropine in the past for these movements without benefit She remains on her depot haloperidol despite the tardive dyskinesia meeting AIMS criteria. The treating psychiatrist is reviewing whether to switch agents Her family is involved and supportive.

data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesia, normal limb tone and reflexes, no tremor, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: AIMS score elevated in oromandibular domain; FBC, UEC, LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Haloperidol 10 mg daily, trial of benztropine without benefit

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase oral benztropine to 4 mg daily for the tardive movements
options.rationale: Anticholinergics do not improve and may worsen TD; benztropine helps acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, not TD. Would be correct in acute dystonia or parkinsonism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Switch from haloperidol to a second-generation antipsychotic, ideally clozapine
options.rationale: Long-term first-generation antipsychotic exposure is the major risk factor for TD; switching to a second-generation antipsychotic with lower TD risk (clozapine has the strongest evidence) is the recommended strategy (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016).

options.text: Add oral risperidone alongside the current haloperidol regimen
options.rationale: Polypharmacy increases adverse-effect burden including TD; combining second D2 antagonist worsens pathology. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Increase haloperidol dose further to suppress the involuntary movements
options.rationale: Increasing offending antipsychotic transiently masks TD but worsens long-term course; contraindicated as management. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Stop all antipsychotic therapy completely and observe over weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal dyskinesia and risks psychotic relapse; switching to lower-risk agent preferred. Would never be correct as planned strategy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: TD presents months to years after antipsychotic use as involuntary orofacial movements. First-line management is to switch to a lower-TD-risk antipsychotic (clozapine has the strongest evidence). VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are emerging but not yet PBS-listed in Australia for routine TD treatment (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
key_points: AIMS assessed 6-monthly in patients on long-term antipsychotics.
Anticholinergics can worsen TD; cease them if possible.
Increasing the offending agent only masks the disorder.
Risk factors: older age, female, first-generation antipsychotics, long duration, prior EPSE.

stem:
A 41-year-old man on clozapine 500 mg nocte for treatment-resistant schizophrenia missed 4 consecutive days of doses while travelling for a family funeral. He is asymptomatic, no longer psychotic, and feels well, but is keen to resume his usual dose tonight. He has a history of one previous generalised tonic-clonic seizure 5 years ago at clozapine 600 mg daily, which prompted dose reduction.

He has no other neurological history. His mother (a nurse) phones the clozapine service requesting advice. Bloods this morning show normal FBC (WCC 6.8, neutrophils 4.0). He takes no other regular medications, weighs 92 kg, has BMI 30, and smokes 20 cigarettes daily. He cannot easily reach the clozapine prescriber until 48 hours from now and his community pharmacy has his usual 500 mg tablet ready The clozapine service consultant on call confirms that any break of more than 48 hours in clozapine requires re-titration from 12.5 mg per the Australian Clozapine Protocols, because the rapid loss of receptor adaptation and the well-known dose-related seizure and cardiovascular risks make restarting at his previous maintenance dose hazardous.

She emphasises that this protocol applies even when the patient feels clinically well and asymptomatic, and that retitration is the same process used at first initiation, with monitoring of vital signs and observation for orthostatic hypotension, sedation, tachycardia and seizure activity during each step.

data_table.Examination: BMI 30, no neurological signs, no fever
data_table.Investigations: WCC 6.8, neutrophils 4.0, UEC normal, glucose 5.8 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 420 ms
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 500 mg nocte (4 doses missed), no other regular meds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart at the usual 500 mg dose tonight without any retitration
options.rationale: After 48+ h without clozapine, tolerance is lost; resuming previous full dose markedly increases orthostatic hypotension, seizure and sedation risk. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

options.text: Resume retitration from 12.5 mg per the standard induction protocol
options.rationale: Australian and manufacturer guidance is that after 2 or more days of missed clozapine doses, the drug must be re-titrated from the starting dose because tolerance to orthostatic hypotension, sedation and seizure risk is rapidly lost; this is particularly important given his prior seizure history (Source: Clozapine product information TGA; eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP).

options.text: Halve the previous dose to 250 mg nocte tonight and resume usual schedule
options.rationale: Halving does not safely re-establish tolerance and still carries significant risk; protocol requires retitration from 12.5 mg. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

options.text: Switch immediately from clozapine to olanzapine at the equivalent oral dose
options.rationale: Switching from clozapine should be planned (relapse risk high); unplanned switch is unsafe and not indicated for missed-dose period. Would never be correct (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Add prophylactic sodium valproate before restarting clozapine at any dose
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant prophylaxis is considered for higher-risk patients during retitration but does not replace requirement to retitrate from start. Would be correct as adjunct, not replacement (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a unique pharmacological profile of rapidly lost tolerance: stopping for as little as 48 hours requires re-titration from the starting dose (12.5 mg) following the standard induction schedule (typically 5-14 days back to therapeutic dose). Restarting at the previous stable dose risks profound hypotension, sedation, anticholinergic delirium, seizures, and cardiac arrhythmia, with reported deaths from medication errors at this transition. Common scenarios prompting re-titration include travel, hospital admission (where clozapine is often omitted due to unfamiliarity), incarceration, refusal during relapse, and supply disruption. The Australian clozapine registry (CPMS or ClopineCentral) coordinates re-initiation: confirm registry status, baseline FBC, ECG, troponin and CRP repeated, then titrate per protocol. During re-titration, weekly FBC, troponin and CRP are required for 4 weeks because myocarditis risk re-emerges with the re-titration window. Patient education on the importance of unbroken supply is part of every clozapine review.
key_points: Restart from 12.5 mg if 2+ days missed; up-titrate cautiously per protocol.
Add prophylactic anticonvulsant in high-risk patients with prior clozapine-related seizures.
Smoking induces CYP1A2; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels.
Communicate any change in smoking, dose or interacting drugs to the clozapine service.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine tolerance is lost rapidly: missed doses for 48 hours or more mandate full re-titration from 12.5 mg, regardless of previous stable dose. Skipping retitration risks hypotension, sedation, seizures and cardiac arrhythmia (TGA Clozapine PI).

stem:
A 64-year-old man admitted 3 days ago for orthopaedic surgery has not received scheduled benzodiazepine prophylaxis despite his documented daily alcohol intake of approximately 20 standard drinks. Last drink was 72 hours ago. He is now confused, agitated, picking at his bedding, and describing animals running across the ceiling. He has had two witnessed brief generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the past 4 hours.

He is febrile, tachycardic, hypertensive, and diaphoretic. CIWA-Ar is now uninterpretable due to confusion. He has a wound dressing intact, no neurological focal deficits, and CT brain is unremarkable. He has received total diazepam 30 mg over the past 6 hours with limited effect. He has known cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B), albumin 28, INR 1.6, AST 130, ALT 70, platelets 95

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 140, BP 174/100, RR 28, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), tremulous, diaphoretic, visual hallucinations, no focal neurology, post-op wound dressed
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.0, Mg 0.58, glucose 5.6, lactate 3.4, INR 1.6, albumin 28, AST 130, ALT 70, platelets 95, CT brain unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Diazepam total 30 mg PO over 6 hours, IV Pabrinex 2 pairs commenced

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Transfer to ICU or HDU, escalate to IV diazepam (or lorazepam if hepatic impairment), correct electrolytes
options.rationale: Delirium tremens with refractory agitation and seizures is a medical emergency requiring high-acuity care; in significant hepatic impairment, lorazepam (less hepatic metabolism, no active metabolites) is preferred over diazepam, with aggressive electrolyte correction (Source: NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines; eTG Addiction; eTG Critical Care).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Continue oral diazepam, increase the frequency and reassess his condition in 4 hours
options.rationale: Oral diazepam in confused, seizing, vomiting patient is unreliable; severe DT requires parenteral therapy and high-acuity monitoring. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 10 mg as the primary treatment for the agitated withdrawal state
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and don't treat underlying GABA deficit; benzodiazepines are first-line in DT with low-dose antipsychotic only as adjunct. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Load with intravenous phenytoin 1 g as primary anti-seizure prophylaxis tonight
options.rationale: Phenytoin is ineffective for alcohol-withdrawal seizures (GABA-mediated); benzodiazepines are both treatment and prophylaxis. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Administer intramuscular naloxone empirically in case of unrecognised opioid involvement
options.rationale: Naloxone has no role in alcohol withdrawal; it is opioid antagonist for opioid overdose. Would never be correct in alcohol withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens has a mortality of 5 to 15% untreated. Australian management is escalation to high-acuity care, parenteral benzodiazepines (lorazepam preferred in significant hepatic impairment because of pharmacokinetics), and aggressive electrolyte correction with high-dose B-complex (Source: NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines).
key_points: DT onset 48 to 96 hours after last drink; mortality without treatment up to 15%.
Lorazepam is preferred over diazepam in significant hepatic dysfunction.
Always replace thiamine before/with glucose and correct magnesium.
Antipsychotics only as adjunct for severe hallucinations after benzodiazepine optimisation.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem:
A 41-year-old woman is referred by her general practitioner to a community psychiatry clinic after 18 months of persistent abdominal pain and fatigue. She has had two normal colonoscopies, a normal gastroscopy, normal abdominal CT, normal coeliac serology, and a normal pelvic ultrasound across this period. She has consulted 11 different clinicians, frequently checks symptom-tracking apps and online forums for several hours each day, and reports that the uncertainty about what is wrong is so distressing that she has reduced her part-time bookkeeping work to one day per week.

She describes the pain as a constant 6 out of 10, worsening with stress, and is convinced something serious has been missed. She denies low mood pervading her day, denies anhedonia, sleeps 6 hours nightly with early waking only when pain is severe, and her K-10 is 24. She uses paracetamol most days and has no other regular medications. She has never had clear hypomanic, psychotic, or panic episodes.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, preoccupied with bodily focus, organised thought, no psychosis. Mild epigastric tenderness, otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 24. FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin all within reference. Two prior colonoscopies and a gastroscopy normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate DSM-5 classification for this presentation?

options.text: Illness anxiety disorder with care-seeking behaviour
options.rationale: Illness anxiety disorder requires preoccupation with HAVING or acquiring a serious illness with minimal or absent somatic symptoms; her dominant feature is the symptoms themselves. Would be correct only with minimal somatic symptoms (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder with persistent course
options.rationale: DSM-5 SSD requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms PLUS disproportionate or persistent thoughts, anxiety, or behaviours about them, for more than 6 months. Her persistent pain, excessive health-related time use, functional decline, and disproportionate concern across 18 months meet criteria; persistent course is specified at >6 months of severe symptoms (DSM-5; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder with somatic predominance
options.rationale: GAD requires excessive worry across multiple domains for 6+ months with 3+ of restlessness/fatigue/concentration/irritability/muscle tension/sleep; somatic symptom focus is the discriminator. Would be correct in multi-domain worry pattern (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Functional neurological disorder, mixed sensory type
options.rationale: FND requires altered voluntary motor/sensory function with positive incompatibility signs (Hoover's, tremor entrainment); abdominal pain and fatigue do not fit. Would be correct with positive incompatibility signs (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self
options.rationale: Factitious requires intentional falsification or induction of signs/symptoms with deceptive intent without obvious external reward; absent here. Would be correct with deception (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 moved decisively away from the 'medically unexplained symptoms' framing of DSM-IV somatoform disorders, recognising that genuine medical conditions and psychiatric distress frequently coexist. Somatic symptom disorder is now defined by the disproportionate cognitive, affective and behavioural response to somatic symptoms: persistent thoughts about seriousness, anxiety, and excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms or health concerns. Symptoms can be medically explained, unexplained, or partially explained - the diagnosis turns on the response, not the aetiology. SSD is a positive diagnosis based on observable clinical features and is made alongside any organic diagnosis rather than as a diagnosis of exclusion. Management is multidisciplinary: a single trusted primary clinician coordinates care, scheduled regular follow-up replaces symptom-driven attendance, investigations are minimised, comorbid mood and anxiety are treated, and CBT for SSD addresses the cognitive-behavioural reaction. Reassurance alone does not work; structured engagement does.
key_points: SSD = >=1 distressing somatic symptom + disproportionate thoughts/anxiety/behaviours + >6 months
Illness anxiety disorder centres on feared disease with little or no somatic symptom
FND requires positive neurological incompatibility signs
Factitious disorder requires deceptive intent without external incentive
explanation.pearls: DSM-5 somatic symptom disorder requires one or more somatic symptoms causing distress or disruption, with disproportionate thoughts, anxiety or time/energy devoted to the symptoms; symptoms can be medically explained or unexplained - the criterion is the disproportionate response, not the absence of explanation (DSM-5; RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

stem:
A 29-year-old graphic designer presents to the emergency department with sudden onset right leg weakness that began 3 days ago after a minor work argument. She has no headache, no visual change, no bowel or bladder symptoms, and no sensory level. She walks with a dragging right leg that appears to swing in a circumduction not typical of pyramidal hemiparesis.

Power in the right hip extensors is 2/5 when tested in isolation, but when she is asked to flex the left hip against resistance while lying supine, you feel strong downward pressure under her right heel. Right knee and ankle reflexes are normal and symmetric, plantar response is flexor, sensation is reported as patchy with a non-anatomical boundary at mid-thigh. Cranial nerves are intact. MRI brain and whole spine completed yesterday are normal. FBC, UEC, glucose, TSH, B12 and HIV serology are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% on air, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Hoover's sign positive on the right (involuntary hip extension during contralateral hip flexion against resistance). Reflexes symmetric, plantars flexor, non-anatomical sensory boundary.
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine normal. FBC, UEC, glucose, TSH, B12, HIV serology normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat MRI brain with stroke protocol and start dual antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: Stroke is unlikely with normal MRI, symmetric reflexes, flexor plantar, positive Hoover's indicating functional weakness; antiplatelets in this setting harms without benefit. Would be correct in confirmed stroke (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Admit for high-dose IV methylprednisolone empirically for suspected multiple sclerosis
options.rationale: MS is excluded by normal MRI and positive functional sign; steroids would entrench illness behaviour. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Tell the patient the scan is normal and there is nothing wrong, with GP follow up in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Telling FND patients 'nothing is wrong' worsens distress, increases relapse and is associated with poorer outcomes; FND is a positive diagnosis to be communicated. Would never be correct (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Explain the positive Hoover's sign as a rule-in diagnosis of functional neurological disorder and refer for FND-specific physiotherapy
options.rationale: FND is a positive diagnosis based on incompatibility signs (Hoover's, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness with normal MRI and reflexes). The first therapeutic step is a clear, non-stigmatising explanation that the diagnosis is made BY the positive sign, framed as a brain functioning problem that is treatable, followed by referral to FND-trained physiotherapy which is the strongest evidence-based intervention (RANZCP; FND Society Consensus; NICE NG217 stroke excluded).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg nocte for somatisation and arrange psychiatric admission
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for FND and inpatient psychiatric admission is rarely indicated; physiotherapy is the evidence-based primary treatment. Would never be correct (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis. Hoover's sign (involuntary recovery of hip extension during contralateral hip flexion) is the bedside test that rules in functional leg weakness. Treatment hinges on a clear non-blaming explanation plus FND-specific physiotherapy (FND Society 2021).
key_points: FND positive signs: Hoover's, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness with normal reflexes
Communicate diagnosis as real, common, and treatable; avoid 'nothing wrong'
FND-specific physiotherapy has the strongest evidence base
Psychological therapy is adjunctive, not primary
explanation.pearls: If MRI is normal AND a positive sign is present, you have rule-in evidence - say so explicitly to the patient (FND Society).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

subtopic_detail: Illness anxiety disorder vs somatic symptom disorder
stem:
A 38-year-old IT consultant attends his general practitioner for the fourth time in 8 weeks requesting another full blood count and tumour marker panel. He is convinced he has pancreatic cancer despite a normal abdominal CT, normal CA 19-9, normal LFTs, and normal pancreatic enzymes obtained 3 weeks ago. He has minor occasional epigastric flutter and mild fatigue but no weight loss, no jaundice, and no anorexia.

He spends 3 to 4 hours daily on patient forums and oncology websites, has read three textbooks on pancreatic cancer staging, and asks colleagues to feel his abdomen for masses. His K-10 is 22. He acknowledges every reassurance gives him relief for around 24 hours before doubt returns. There is no family history of pancreatic cancer. He has no other regular medications. He sleeps 6 hours and his weight is stable. His functional decline at work is described as moderate.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, pressured speech around health topics, no thought disorder. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, lipase, CA 19-9 all within reference. Abdominal CT 3 weeks ago: normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain
options.rationale: SSD requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms as focus; his somatic symptoms are minor and dominant feature is fear of having pancreatic cancer. Would be correct with predominant somatic symptoms (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder, severe
options.rationale: GAD requires worry across multiple domains for 6+ months; his worry is narrowly focused on single feared disease (illness anxiety pattern). Would be correct in multi-domain worry (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Illness anxiety disorder, care-seeking type
options.rationale: DSM-5 illness anxiety disorder: preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness; somatic symptoms are absent or mild; high health-related anxiety; excessive health-related behaviours OR maladaptive avoidance; duration >=6 months; not better explained by another disorder. Repeated investigations, reassurance-seeking, and forum use mark the care-seeking type (DSM-5; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder with contamination obsessions
options.rationale: OCD requires obsessions and/or compulsions consuming over 1 hour daily; his behaviours are health-focused reassurance-seeking, not classical OCD. Would be correct with classical OCD obsessions (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Delusional disorder, somatic type
options.rationale: Delusional disorder somatic type requires fixed false beliefs of bodily disease with delusional intensity; he accepts reassurance partially. Would be correct with delusional intensity (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

explanation.summary: Illness anxiety disorder is dominated by fear of having or acquiring a serious illness with minimal somatic symptoms; SSD is dominated by distressing somatic symptoms themselves. Discriminator: 'is the patient distressed by the symptom or by what the symptom means?' (DSM-5).
key_points: IAD: feared disease + minimal somatic symptoms + >6 months + health-related behaviours
Care-seeking type repeatedly investigates; care-avoidant type avoids medical contact
Reassurance provides only short-term relief, a hallmark feature
Differentiate from delusional disorder by reality testing
explanation.pearls: If reassurance helps for 24 hours then doubt returns, think illness anxiety, not delusion (RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to ED for the 7th time in 8 months with recurrent hypoglycaemia (plasma glucose 2.1-2.6 mmol/L, markedly elevated insulin and SUPPRESSED C-peptide each time). He has no diabetes, no insulinoma on prior CT and MRI. He is a former endocrinology nurse, currently unemployed, lives alone. He denies injecting insulin and becomes irritable when asked. He has no pending litigation, no Centrelink claim under reviewo active forensic process.

Staff have observed him discarding small objects in the sharps bin after symptom onset. Each admission has involved invasive investigations and extended stays during which he is highly engaged with treating teams who describe him as 'the most knowledgeable patient we've ever had'. He receives no financial benefit from admissions but openly enjoys the medical-team attention. K-10 is 30 with profound loneliness.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 128/82, RR 16, BSL 2.3 mmol/L on arrival.
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, oriented, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Plasma glucose 2.3 mmol/L, insulin 480 pmol/L (markedly raised), C-peptide 90 pmol/L (suppressed), sulfonylurea screen negative. CT and MRI pancreas previously normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate DSM-5 classification of his behaviour?

options.text: Malingering for secondary financial gain
options.rationale: Malingering requires EXTERNAL incentive (financial, legal, evasion of duty, drug-seeking); he has no claim, litigation, forensic process. Would be correct with external incentive (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: DSM-5-TR Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self
options.rationale: Three DSM-5 criteria are met: (i) falsification of physical signs (covertly self-administered insulin, evidenced by suppressed C-peptide with elevated insulin and observed sharps disposal); (ii) presentation as ill/injured/impaired; (iii) absence of obvious external incentive. The internal psychological gain (sick-role identity, relational connection with medical teams) is the discriminator from malingering and is consistent with his nursing-background insider-knowledge profile.

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain
options.rationale: SSD involves genuine somatic symptoms with disproportionate thoughts/feelings/behaviours; deliberate falsification takes case out of SSD. Would be correct with genuine symptoms (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)
options.rationale: Conversion requires neurological symptoms (weakness, tremor, sensory loss) without organic cause; biochemical hypoglycaemia is not neurological. Would be correct with neurological symptoms (Source: DSM-5).

options.text: Delusional disorder, somatic type
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires fixed false belief; he is engaged in covert behaviour (sharps disposal) implying awareness of deception, inconsistent with delusional intensity. Would be correct with delusional intensity (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Factitious disorder vs malingering hinges on motivation: factitious is intentional symptom production motivated by the sick role with NO external incentive; malingering is intentional symptom production for external incentive (benefits, avoidance, drugs). Suppressed C-peptide with elevated insulin is a textbook signature of surreptitious insulin use (DSM-5; AMH).
key_points: Factitious disorder: intentional + deceptive + no external incentive (sick-role motive)
Malingering: intentional + deceptive + external incentive
Suppressed C-peptide + high insulin + negative sulfonylurea = exogenous insulin
Approach: avoid confrontation, address underlying psychological need, consult-liaison referral
explanation.pearls: Document objective evidence of induction (lab pattern, hidden items) before formulating - confrontation typically escalates the behaviour (RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

stem:
A 52-year-old woman is referred to community mental health by her general practitioner for a 4-month history of fatigue, low mood, weight gain of 5 kg, constipation, cold intolerance, and reduced concentration. She has stopped her weekly bushwalking group and finds her brain feels foggy. Her sister has Hashimoto thyroiditis and her mother had pernicious anaemia. She has no prior psychiatric history, no suicidal ideation, and her affect is flat with mildly slowed thought tempo.

She is not pregnant. She takes no regular medications and drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. Her general practitioner started sertraline 50 mg daily 6 weeks ago without baseline bloods, with no improvement, and has now sent her with K-10 of 28. On examination her skin is dry, reflexes show delayed relaxation phase, and there is a small diffuse non-tender goitre. HR is 52.

data_table.Examination: Slow speech, flat affect, dry skin, delayed reflex relaxation, small diffuse goitre.
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed by mental health team.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation before adjusting psychotropic therapy?

options.text: Switch sertraline to mirtazapine 30 mg nocte and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Switching antidepressants without first excluding medical mimic risks treating thyroid disease as treatment-resistant depression; AMH and RANZCP mandate exclusion of medical cause. Would never be correct without thyroid workup (Source: RANZCP).

options.text: Dexamethasone suppression test for Cushing syndrome
options.rationale: Cushing screening is for features suggestive of cortisol excess (central adiposity, striae, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia); absent here. Would be correct with Cushing features (Source: APEG).

options.text: Brain MRI to exclude frontal lobe lesion
options.rationale: MRI not first-line with clear thyroid-pointing physical findings and no focal neurology; low pre-test probability. Would be correct with focal neuro findings (Source: RANZCR).

options.text: TSH, free T4 and thyroid peroxidase antibodies
options.rationale: Clinical features (bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation, goitre, cold intolerance, weight gain, family history of autoimmune thyroid disease) point to primary hypothyroidism, most likely Hashimoto. TSH plus free T4 is the screening pair; TPO antibodies confirm autoimmune aetiology and guide monitoring of subclinical disease. RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines require excluding thyroid disease before labelling depression as primary (RANZCP; eTG).
